overclaims: F1 (landing quantile) is a relabelled margin: today's fixed 2 s is already the 20th percentile of the measured error on held reads in all four campaign 34 arms and within 1-4 % of the best cost near lambda / c = 2e-5 (ev_fetch). The rule moves mean TTFT by at most 0.013 s weighted by c and about 1 % of the host pool; at saturation q is a ratio of two numbers near zero and needs a clamp.

F2 and F3 change nothing at campaign 34: the existing GPU-bound filter already decides the same way (wait >= read in 3,929 of 3,973 'arrival' decisions, re-counted here; 1 staged read in the run). F3 alone turns 412 decisions into early reads at saturation and is +0.31 s on the workflow's simulator. Claim them as one guard, not a gain.

F4 (read or recompute by price) is worth at most 0.004 s per returning request with perfect choice and loses when keyed on an idle GPU (ev_prices); it is +4.0 s on the simulator. Section 2's 'recompute always wins on an idle FA3 GPU' is wrong: the request's own times tie near 44-55 K tokens.
F5 is a defect fix (a lookup is charged before its result), worth 0.007-0.16 s plus 6-13 ms per returning turn at light load. It is not derived from the prices.

R1 saves 4.6-4.8 % of write tokens and under 1 % of device time at saturation, with no TTFT effect. R2, R3, R5 and P2 have nothing to act on at campaign 34: writes are acked in 0.6-0.8 s, no write was acked short in six arms, no unstored unlocked page exists, and the reserve rule would hold 0 times. What removed campaign 32's condition was merging (fix 2). They are guards.

P1 has no measurable effect on the mean: 0 soft-pin bumps in campaigns 32 and 34, and its target (111-171 queued turns per half hour that lose resident history) sits where c = 0, so by the draft's own identity it moves who waits. Claim it on readers' p90, after a repeat run.

PR1 and the title: at every measured operating point lambda is 1-2e-7 or about 0, kappa is 0 as a price, c is nearly binary and the engine's price never moved. Only mu is large, and section 6 states it three times too low (1 + ready turns against N - B = 109). The three prices decide nothing in campaigns 32 to 34, and the room that is dearest at saturation, the GPU pool, has no price in the draft.

R4 as written ('ended sessions' chains first') makes the SSD tier worse (3.6-4.0 s against 1.6-1.9 s, ev_ssd); the form that works keeps first prompts and refreshes on lookup hits. Its 1.6-1.9 s is inferred through the identity: the late TTFT rise starts at minute 85-86, before the first pass.

Optimality and any distance from a floor: each rule is exact for a priced single-session problem; under hard capacity the index order is a heuristic and weak duality fails in the saturated closed loop. A floor built on today's GPU seconds per request takes as given that 8-12 % of them are a prefill pass waiting on the host-to-GPU copy, that 2-3 % of the GPU pool idles behind a head that does not fit, and that the cleaner's scan slows the loop 17-39 % for 11 s per pass. On the simulator the copy wait alone is worth 1.9-4.2 s of a 10.6 s mean, several times the 0.4-0.5 s the draft's candidates can still move.

Section 1.2: the load is not 'about 0.4 s'. The copy takes 57-66 ms per request (2.5 us a token); 0.4 s is the wait for pool room after a landing. Recompute cost is not 'nearly constant in the context length': cold prefill grows with position (25 us a token at 8 K, 59 us at 64 K; seam_fp, ev_prices). Section 2's '0.9 s of lags' are seeds; an uncontended read measures 0.05 s plus 0.044 ms a token.

Section 3.3: campaign 26 does not support the falling-hazard explanation. Its hints were sharp (p90/p10 median 3.7, hazard still rising within a read time for 86 % of readers' entries; ev_fetch). The paper should name which setting exercises the rising-hazard case.

Section 4.2: '56 to 67 % of prompt positions are read back' is 38-49 % of submitted tokens and 51-66 % of live sessions' prompt pages (ev_write). 'With an idle device, write at once (it is free)' leaves out wear: 3.0 TB written in 2 h to a 2.5 TB device.
Section 4.3: the mirror is not held 'for nothing'. It is what keeps GPU eviction from waiting on a copy: on the simulator dropping it is -0.22 s if the copy were free and +7.8 s with the copy inline.

Section 5.2: the 50 K / 25 K hold is not 'one threshold of this comparison'. At every hold but one it counted prompt pages of a request still running, which hold nothing eviction could take (ev_write).

Section 7 item 8: 'N g' should read (N - B) g, and 'same GPU work per request means the same mean TTFT whatever the read timing' is contradicted on one run per arm by jit_p50 (+0.8 to +1.3 s of TTFT for +3.2 s of stall; ev_prices). Item 9's stability claim should be stated in transfers, not tokens (ev_write).

Evidence base: one run per arm, arms within 0.7 s, and the saturated setting's run-to-run spread was never measured; on the simulator the arrival draw alone moves ec_full's mean between 8.8 and 19.0 s over three seeds. Everything is one GPU with TP = 1, bf16 KV, one mixture-of-experts model, replies never re-sent and output lengths known to admission. State these beside every gain.
ranked_build_list: 1. Load pass-over (new; Fetch and Preempt on the GPU tier). Start a turn's host-to-GPU copy when it is chosen for admission, keep decoding, and prefill the turn once the copy's event is done (unified_radix_cache.py:3980 has the gate, :3806 the cross-rank count). Largest expected effect by far: 8-12 % of GPU time at saturation, 1.9-4.2 s of a 10.6 s mean on the simulator (inferred). Medium effort in the scheduler's admission loop. Needs a GPU A/B at campaign 34's setting and a repeat for spread. First step with no risk: log the copy wait per admission.

2. R4 in ev_ssd's form, with X1's explicit-end predicate: touch on lookup hits, then the three file-time classes, and the re-check before unlink. Add: take the cleaner's scan out of the scheduler's process (new). Removes 0.33 s over the run (1.6-1.9 s late, inferred) and 0.1-0.3 s of scan slowdown while passes run.

3. First-fit admission among ready turns with a bound on skips (new; Preempt on GPU room). About 2 % of the pool, 0.3 s on the simulator. A few lines at scheduler.py:4045-4072; check long-context turns' p90.
4. F5, way B then way A, with the scheduler's second re-issue budget counted the same way: 0.007-0.16 s and 6-13 ms per returning turn at light load.
5. P1 by rank (ready turns ahead, the first k chains locked) with X2, not by a time slack. Readers' tail and re-read volume only; no mean effect to claim.

6. PR1 as a log line only, with mu = N - B, a GPU-room price, copy-wait ms and bytes written; replace the Triton recompute constant and the 0.9 s lag seeds by fits. No decision should read lambda or kappa at saturation.
7. Shared heads ranked by their own time between uses (new, small): 63 % of first requests' reusable tokens come from the SSD today; about 2.5 % less read volume, TTFT about 0.
8. For tight host pools and for wear (campaign 37 and after): mirror reclaim and writes at their due date, both only once copies run beside decode (step 1); R1 goes with them.
9. F1, F2 with F3, R2, R3, R5, P2: guards behind switches if wanted; no gain to claim at campaigns 32 to 34. Leave F4 off.

10. Before any claim: one repeat of the saturated setting for the spread, and the scope stated (one GPU, TP = 1, bf16 KV). FP8 KV and TP > 1 are untested and would change the number of running requests and every byte rate.
